canonicalExplanation.summary: A **branch** is not a folder or a copy of your files. It's a **name that points at one commit**, stored as a tiny file containing a hash. All branches share one commit graph. When you commit, **the branch you're on moves forward** to the new commit; other branches stay put. **HEAD** says where you are: normally it points at a branch (`HEAD -> feature`), so commits move that branch. If you check out a commit directly, HEAD is **detached**: new commits belong to no branch and are easy to lose, so create a branch first with `git switch -c`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner creates a branch called feature, expecting Git to copy the project somewhere. The folder looks identical, so they're confused about what changed. They commit, switch back to main, and their new file vanishes, then reappears when they switch back. Committing on feature moves the feature reference to the new commit while main continues to point at its previous commit. In this lesson you'll draw and manipulate a small branch graph while predicting HEAD movement.

```predict
{"question": "You run `git branch feature` on main. How many new commits exist?", "options": ["One, a copy of main", "Zero: feature is just a new name pointing at the same commit"], "answer": 1, "why": "Creating a branch writes a pointer, nothing more. That's why it's instant."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Commits and history** (snapshots with parents) and **Log, show and graph** (reading git log --graph output).

sections.heading: The model: names pointing into one graph
sections.body:
```bash
git switch -c feature          # create feature at the current commit and move HEAD to it.
echo "hi" > hello.txt
git add hello.txt && git commit -m "Add greeting"
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate
# * 9e1f0a2 (HEAD -> feature) Add greeting
# * 5b2c7d4 (main) Initial commit

git switch main                # HEAD -> main; hello.txt leaves the working tree.
cat .git/refs/heads/feature    # just a hash (may be packed in .git/packed-refs).
```

```text
before:   A (main, feature, HEAD->feature)
after:    A (main) --- B (feature, HEAD->feature)
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "What is detached HEAD?", "answer": "HEAD points straight at a commit instead of a branch, for example after `git switch --detach 5b2c7d4`. Commits made there move no branch; run `git switch -c rescue` to give them a name before leaving."}
```

sections.heading: Predict the pointer

includes: Explain branches as movable names for commits in one shared graph.
Predict how commits move the current branch and what detached HEAD means.

outcomes: Draw and manipulate a small branch graph while predicting HEAD movement.

examples.title: Committing on feature
examples.situation: Committing on feature moves the feature reference to the new commit while main continues to point at its previous commit.
walkthrough: **Create:** git switch -c feature points a new name at the same commit as main.
**Committing on feature moves the feature reference:** after "Add greeting", feature points to the new commit 9e1f0a2.
**Main continues to point at its previous commit:** switching to main will remove hello.txt from the working tree, because main's commit lacks it.
examples.result: The learner sees branches as pointers, and the vanishing file makes sense.

examples.title: The lost detached commits
examples.situation: A learner checks out an old commit to test something, commits a fix, then switches to main. The fix seems gone.
walkthrough: HEAD was detached, so no branch moved to the fix commit.
Git printed the commit's hash when leaving; git reflog also lists it.
git branch rescue <hash> gives it a name and brings it back.
examples.result: The fix is recovered, and next time the learner runs git switch -c before committing.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A branch contains its own copied files and commits rather than naming one position in a shared commit graph.
misconceptions.correction: A branch is a pointer to one commit. Files come from whichever commit is checked out, and commits are shared by every branch that can reach them.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, how many commits did git branch feature create?

analogy.example: Branches are like **sticky notes on pages of one notebook**. Writing a new page while holding the "feature" note moves that note to the new page. The "main" note stays where it was. HEAD is **your finger**, showing which note you're holding.
limitations: Real notebooks are linear; Git's graph can split and join.
Pages with no note (detached commits) are easy to lose.

steps.explanation: A new name points at the same commit as main.
Committing on feature moves the feature reference to the new commit.
Main continues to point at its previous commit.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing branch pointers. Step 1, Create: main is A; feature is A; HEAD is feature. A new name points at the same commit as main. Step 2, Commit: feature is B; main is A. Committing on feature moves the feature reference to the new commit. Step 3, Switch: HEAD is main; working tree is commit A files. Main continues to point at its previous commit.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable repo, draw the graph on paper, then create two branches, commit once on each, and check your drawing with git log --oneline --graph --all.

farTransfer.prompt: Deliberately create a detached HEAD, make a commit, switch away, then recover the commit using the hash Git printed or git reflog. Explain each pointer's position at every step.
expectedEvidence: Commit recovered onto a named branch.

remediation.explanation: Before each commit or switch, answer: **where does HEAD point, and which branch will move?** Check with git status's first line.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The lost detached commits".

recap.summary: To draw and manipulate a branch graph, treat each branch as a movable name for one commit in a shared graph, remember only the branch HEAD points to moves when you commit, and create a branch before committing on a detached HEAD.
